subject: math
description: Students prove and apply the key fact behind the elimination (linear combination) method: given a system of two equations in two variables, replacing one equation with the sum of that equation and a nonzero multiple of the other produces an equivalent system with exactly the same solution set. They justify why this replacement preserves solutions, choose multipliers that eliminate a variable, generate equivalent systems, and recognize when two systems are (or are not) equivalent.
subSkills: State and use the replacement principle: $E_1$ may be replaced by $E_1 + k\,E_2$ (for $k \neq 0$) without changing the solution set
Verify that a given ordered pair satisfying a system also satisfies the new (combined) equation, and vice versa
Choose a multiplier $k$ so that adding $k$ times one equation to the other eliminates a chosen variable
Multiply both sides of an equation by a nonzero constant correctly (distribute over every term)
Form the sum $a\,E_1 + b\,E_2$ of two equations term by term
Decide whether two systems are equivalent by checking that one row is a linear combination of the original rows (and the other row is preserved)
Explain the logical 'if and only if' reasoning: any solution of the original system is a solution of the replacement, and any solution of the replacement is a solution of the original

problemArchetypes.name: Verify a replacement preserves a known solution
problemArchetypes.example: The system $\begin{cases} 2x + 3y = 12 \\ x - y = 1 \end{cases}$ has solution $(3, 2)$. Replace the first equation with $(2x+3y) + 2(x-y) = 12 + 2(1)$, giving $4x + y = 14$. Show that $(3,2)$ still satisfies the new system.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose a multiplier to eliminate a variable
problemArchetypes.example: For $\begin{cases} 3x + 4y = 10 \\ x - 2y = -4 \end{cases}$, what multiple $k$ of the second equation should be added to the first so that $y$ is eliminated? (Answer: $k = 2$, giving $5x = 2$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Generate the new equivalent equation from a stated combination
problemArchetypes.example: Given $\begin{cases} 5x - 2y = 7 \\ 3x + y = 9 \end{cases}$, write the equation obtained by replacing the first equation with $E_1 + 2E_2$. (Answer: $11x = 25$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Decide whether two systems are equivalent
problemArchetypes.example: Is $\begin{cases} x + y = 5 \\ 2x + 5y = 16 \end{cases}$ equivalent to $\begin{cases} x + y = 5 \\ 3y = 6 \end{cases}$? Justify by showing the second row of the new system equals $E_2 - 2E_1$ of the original.

problemArchetypes.name: Prove/justify the replacement principle in general
problemArchetypes.example: Explain why, for any $k$, every solution $(x_0, y_0)$ of $\begin{cases} E_1 \\ E_2 \end{cases}$ is also a solution of $\begin{cases} E_1 + kE_2 \\ E_2 \end{cases}$, and why every solution of the new system solves the original. Identify the property (a true equation stays true when equal quantities are added) that makes this work.

problemArchetypes.name: Solve a system by a full linear-combination chain
problemArchetypes.example: Use the replacement principle to solve $\begin{cases} 2x + 3y = 4 \\ 4x - y = 22 \end{cases}$: replace $E_2$ with $E_2 - 2E_1$ to get $-7y = 14$, so $y = -2$ and $x = 5$.

Easy.description: Single-step replacement or verification with a supplied multiplier. The student either checks that a stated combination keeps a given solution, or forms the sum of two equations when one is already lined up to eliminate a variable with multiplier $1$ or $-1$.
constraints: Multiplier is supplied or is $\pm 1$ (no scaling decision required)
Integer coefficients with absolute value $\le 6$; a variable already cancels by direct addition or subtraction
Tasks are 'verify $(x_0,y_0)$ still works' or 'write $E_1 + E_2$'
tier1 lower band: confirm-the-solution and direct-sum items live here

Medium.description: Student must choose a single nonzero multiplier to eliminate a variable, then form the combined equation correctly, distributing the multiplier across every term including the constant.
constraints: Requires selecting $k$ (a small integer, $|k| \le 4$) so one variable's coefficients become opposites
Must multiply both sides of one equation before adding; common arithmetic on integer coefficients
Includes 'are these two systems equivalent?' items where one row is a single combination of the originals
tier1 upper band / tier2 lower band: this is the natural split point between the two worksheets

Hard.description: Multi-step reasoning: combinations may require scaling BOTH equations (e.g. $aE_1 + bE_2$), proving the if-and-only-if equivalence in general (not just one direction), or carrying out a full solve-and-justify chain. May involve fractional or larger coefficients and an explanation of why a zero multiplier is excluded.
constraints: Both equations may need a multiplier ($aE_1 + bE_2$ with $a, b \neq 0$)
Coefficients may be larger or fractional; answers given as exact fractions such as $\frac{2}{5}$
Requires a written justification of both directions of the equivalence, or identifying why $k = 0$ fails to preserve the system
tier2 upper band: general proof and multi-step solve-and-prove items

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student multiplies only the side of the equation with the variables and forgets to multiply the constant term
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $2(x - y) = 1$ within $E_1 + 2E_2$, writes $4x + y = 12$ instead of $4x + y = 14$ because $2 \cdot 1$ was dropped

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes any replacement (including replacing an equation by a multiple of itself or by $E_1 + 0\cdot E_2$) gives an equivalent system, ignoring the nonzero-multiplier requirement
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims replacing $E_1$ with $0 \cdot E_1 + 0 \cdot E_2 = 0$ keeps the solution set, or that scaling an equation by $0$ is allowed

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds the multiplier to the equation instead of multiplying the equation by it
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $E_1 + 2E_2$ treats it as $E_1 + (E_2 + 2)$, producing $5x - 2y = 9$ instead of $11x = 25$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses a multiplier that scales the wrong variable's coefficients, so nothing eliminates
commonMisconceptions.distractor: To eliminate $y$ from $3x + 4y = 10$ and $x - 2y = -4$, picks $k = 1$ (giving $4x + 2y = 6$) instead of $k = 2$, leaving $y$ present

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reverses the sign when subtracting one equation from another (sign error across the whole equation)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $E_2 - 2E_1$ of $4x - y = 22$ and $2x + 3y = 4$, writes $-7y = 30$ instead of $-7y = 14$ by mis-signing the constant

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks the combined equation alone (one equation) is the equivalent 'system' and drops the second, preserved equation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: States the system $\begin{cases} E_1 + kE_2 \\ E_2 \end{cases}$ is equivalent to the single equation $E_1 + kE_2$, losing a solution constraint

_comment_itemCounts: Standard model: one lesson (5 worked + 5 practice), one ramped single worksheet of 15 (Easy verification -> Hard general proof), one quiz of 8 multiple-choice. tier1/tier2 sizes are recorded per schema but this standard uses the single ramped worksheet.
